Obsidian’s Official Skills Are Here! It’s time to let AI plug into your local Vault.

Kurtis Redux

Obsidian Just Did the Most “Obsidian” Thing

Recently, Obsidian’s CEO Steph Ango (better known as kepano) did something gloriously, quintessentially Obsidian. Instead of cramming an “Ask AI” button into the UI like so many SaaS apps do, he released an open-source repo called “Obsidian Skills” that teaches AI how to use Obsidian properly.

Why does this have me, genuinely excited? Because it’s a perfect example of the “toolchain” philosophy I keep advocating. Let each tool do its job and play nicely with others — don’t roll everything into one bloated super app. Obsidian has always walked this talk: starting with local Markdown and open formats so it could slot cleanly into a toolchain rather than own every step.

Below, I’ll introduce the Skills concept and how to use Obsidian Skills. It might feel a bit technical if you’re not a developer, but in my view this is the best moment to get onboard. I’ve held off installing those sketchy third-party AI plugins for Obsidian for a reason — this is the approach I’ve been waiting for.

What Are “Skills,” Exactly?

Here, “Skills” refers to Claude Code’s Agent Skills mechanism. In short:

  • You drop a set of instruction files (a simple text format — looks like YAML) into a specific directory.
  • Claude first loads each skill’s name and description.
  • When your request matches a skill’s description, that skill activates and Claude follows the rules in that file for subsequent actions.

Skills may have started as a developer feature, but they’re useful far beyond coding. Knowledge workers can benefit just as much.

For example, suppose you’ve defined a skill for generating a standard web UI layout. You tell the AI, “Design a login page,” and it checks your Skills first, like reading the manual, then produces the page using your standards.

The key point: Skills are not plugins. They don’t require migrating your data into a proprietary app database. They’re portable rulebooks, really. That aligns perfectly with Obsidian’s DNA: human-readable text files you control, open formats, and tools cooperating via clear rules.

What’s in Obsidian Skills: The Three File Types AI Most Often Messes Up

kepano’s open-source repo is called kepano/obsidian-skills and is MIT-licensed.

Installation is simple: place the repo contents in a /.claude folder at the root of your Obsidian vault (or in the working directory you use with Claude Code).

Today, Obsidian Skills covers three major Obsidian file types:

1) Obsidian-Flavored Markdown (.md)

The most common AI faceplant is “treating Obsidian like a generic Markdown editor”:

  • Using normal links instead of [[wikilinks]]
  • Getting embed syntax wrong
  • Mixing up properties vs frontmatter
  • Ignoring Obsidian-specific behaviors and features

This skill nudges the AI to output Markdown that’s truly “Obsidian-flavored.”

2) Obsidian Bases (.base)

Bases are classic Obsidian: “looks like a database, still just files.” A .base file defines views, filters, formulas, rollups, etc., so you can browse notes as tables or cards in Obsidian. Without strict guidance, AI tends to bungle field names, nesting, or structure. The skill keeps it on the rails.

3) JSON Canvas (.canvas)

Canvas is backed by the open JSON Canvas format (Obsidian even published a spec). A .canvas file is JSON with a fixed schema for nodes, connections, and groups. Without rules, AI will forget fields or nest things incorrectly. This skill teaches it to comply with the schema.

Side note: the repo started getting commits on 2026–01–02 (the first two were Obsidian Markdown and Bases), with JSON Canvas, plugin metadata, and directory fixes landing shortly after.

How Can We Use It?

Let’s start with the fun part — results.

  • Say: “Create an Obsidian Canvas to briefly explain the MCP concept.” The AI will invoke the Canvas skill and generate a valid .canvas file you can open in Obsidian right away.
  • Or: “List the top 10 paintings in world art history with short descriptions, and store them in an Obsidian Base.” The AI will create a .base file with the right structure.

Hands-On Steps

Here’s the catch: the Skills mechanism is easy to grasp, but getting it working involves a bunch of practical steps that can scare off newcomers — especially because many folks can’t (or don’t want to) use Claude Code directly. Obsidian Skills is designed around the Claude Code standard.

I suspect this traces back to Anthropic’s approach. Skills (and the previously buzzy MCP, Model Context Protocol) are open standards proposed by Anthropic. Open standards are great, but at the product layer they still seem to funnel you into Anthropic’s platform. Recently, there was also news that OpenCode (an open-source alternative to Claude Code) ran into restrictions from Anthropic. Personally, I don’t like mission-critical tools being held by a single company. Longtime readers know my stance: tools with real exit options are good tools; tools that want to lock you in are a risk to your workflow.

With that out of the way, here’s a streamlined path. Expect rough edges — someone will probably turn this into a paid course or white-glove service soon enough.

1) Pick a Claude Code alternative

You’ve got options, both domestic and international. I recommend going open-source where possible to protect local data. Since OpenCode was reportedly targeted, let’s use it as the example. Goose is also solid and highly compatible with Claude Code.

After installing, connect it to a model you like (that’s the point of openness: you’re not forced to use Anthropic’s own model). OpenCode even supports several strong domestic models. If you’re new to AI, picking a model is a long discussion — I’ll skip it here.

Note: Claude Code and its alternatives started life as AI dev assistants. They’re heavy for Obsidian use — lots of commands you won’t need — but they can still drive the Skills workflow just fine.

2) Load the Skills

Install OpenCode (or any compatible client/CLI). Grab Obsidian Skills from GitHub and copy it into your Obsidian vault at /.claude/ (or the path your tool expects).

Many AI tools are smart enough to install Skills for you if you say, “Fetch the Skills from repo X and install them in folder Y.” But you still need to provide correct source and target paths, which is about as much work as doing it manually. Pick whichever approach you prefer.

3) Set the working directory

OpenCode may need you to set a working directory. You can also mention your Obsidian vault path explicitly in a prompt. Otherwise, how would the AI know where to write files or which conventions to follow?

The simplest approach: run OpenCode from the root of your vault so the current path is correct by default. You can make a shortcut or script with parameters for one-click access later.

4) Get to work

Now just ask for what you want. For example:
“Inside the Drafts folder, use the Obsidian Canvas skill to generate a canvas introducing the major planets and moons of the Solar System.”

Final Thoughts

What’s delightful about kepano’s release is that it’s not “bolting AI into the product.” It’s a skill pack that explains Obsidian’s file grammars clearly. Obsidian continues to champion open formats (Markdown, .base, JSON Canvas), and AI becomes just another optional tool that reads and writes those formats. You choose your platform. You choose your model. That’s what I mean by having “options.”

This week has me fired up. Obsidian’s move brings AI one step closer to knowledge workers, not just developers. Why keep paying for flashy-but-mediocre cloud-wrapped SaaS AI tools? The AI novelty has worn off — it’s time for practicality. Either be truly innovative and specialized (like some focused online AI tools), or become a reliable link in a toolchain — like Obsidian. Otherwise, what real value do the bloated, “do-everything” AI suites have beyond marketing hype?
